title: Chapter XXII
focus: the wedding night and its catastrophe

teacherSummary.text: Victor and Elizabeth marry and travel to Evian. Armed and expecting to be attacked himself, Victor leaves Elizabeth alone, and the creature murders her. Victor's father dies of grief, and a Genevan magistrate doubts Victor's story.

vocabulary.definition: To tax or to task too heavily
vocabulary.context: I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength, and that I must repose before I could continue my journey.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overtax”: vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To free from chains or slavery
vocabulary.context: I had unchained an enemy among them, whose joy it was to shed their blood, and to revel in their groans.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unchain”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: He wished as much as possible to obliterate the memory of the scenes that had taken place in Ireland, and never alluded to them, or suffered me to speak of my misfortunes.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “obliterate”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + liter (Latin littera, "letter") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: When reason returned, she would remonstrate, and endeavour to inspire me with resignation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “remonstrate”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An oval or circular building with rising tiers of seats about an open space called the arena
vocabulary.context: The Alps here come closer to the lake, and we approached the amphitheatre of mountains which forms its eastern boundary.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “amphitheatre”: the (Greek theos, "god"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Victor, be assured that your cousin and playmate has too sincere a love for you not to be made miserable by this supposition.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “playmate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To be placed in a center
vocabulary.context: I said, “little happiness remains for us on earth; yet all that I may one day enjoy is centred in you.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “centre”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “futility”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Alas! what freedom? such as the peasant enjoys when his family have been massacred before his eyes, his cottage burnt, his lands laid waste, and he is turned adrift, homeless, penniless, and alone, but free.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “penniless”: -less (Old English -leas, "without"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I resolved, therefore, that if my immediate union with my cousin would conduce either to hers or my father’s happiness, my adversary’s designs against my life should not retard it a single hour.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conduce”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + duc (Latin ducere, "to lead"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Weddings in this social class involved property arrangements; the Frankensteins regain some of Elizabeth's inheritance.

significance: Dramatic irony: readers suspect the danger is to Elizabeth while Victor thinks only of himself.
discussionQuestions: Why does Victor misread the threat?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

items.prompt: Where do the newlyweds spend their wedding night?
Who is killed on the wedding night?
Who did Victor expect the creature to attack?
How does the magistrate respond to Victor's story?
In the line “I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength, and that I must repose before I could continue my journey.”, what does “overtaxed” most nearly mean?
options: To tax or to task too heavily
To free from chains or slavery

items.prompt: In the line “I had unchained an enemy among them, whose joy it was to shed their blood, and to revel in their groans.”, what does “unchained” most nearly mean?

To free from chains or slavery

answerKey.answer: To tax or to task too heavily
To free from chains or slavery

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXII,” how does Shelley show the wedding night and its catastrophe? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXII, how does Shelley develop the idea of the wedding night and its catastrophe? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXII develops the idea of the wedding night and its catastrophe. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of the wedding night and its catastrophe. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXII suggests about the wedding night and its catastrophe. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter XXII to complicate the reader's understanding of the wedding night and its catastrophe. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the wedding night and its catastrophe responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the wedding night and its catastrophe follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXII and its treatment of the wedding night and its catastrophe. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXII as evidence for a larger claim about the wedding night and its catastrophe in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the wedding night and its catastrophe. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events
annotationFocus.passage: My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society, and strove by various arguments to banish my despair. Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Victor misread the threat? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are overtaxed, unchained, obliterate, remonstrate, amphitheatre. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength, and that I must repose before I could continue my journey.” Webster's says: To tax or to task too heavily. Now the word history: “overtax”: vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “unchain”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “obliterate”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + liter (Latin littera, "letter") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Weddings in this social class involved property arrangements; the Frankensteins regain some of Elizabeth's inheritance. Why does this chapter matter? Dramatic irony: readers suspect the danger is to Elizabeth while Victor thinks only of himself. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the wedding night and its catastrophe.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Irony, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society, and strove by various arguments to banish my despair. Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Irony, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXII,” how does Shelley show the wedding night and its catastrophe? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the wedding night and its catastrophe, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes the wedding night and its catastrophe. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
